title: Wild Hikers Need More Respect for Nature
subtitle: China Newsweek July 13, 2026
paragraphs: Despite growing popularity for

outdoor activities involving about 400 million participants across China, the most desirable destinations have closed access to off-trail trekkers. After the number of accidents soared by 41.2 percent year-on-year and pollution and trash threaten the environment of nature reserves, local governments have expanded prohibited zones. However, their one-size-fits-all measures such as encircling nature reserves with razor wire not only fail to deter trekkers, but also jeopardize wildlife by fragmenting their habitats. China's hiking boom started at the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, and with the number of trekkers having tripled from 2020 to 2024, professional hikers and local officials agree that sound development of the outdoor sports industry depends on people's respect for nature.

title: FIFA World Cup Sponsors Gain Popularity
subtitle: Yi Magazine July 9, 2026
paragraphs: Involving newcomers, offline promotions and global strategies, FIFA World Cup sponsorship in China boomed, even though the Chinese men's team consistently fails to reach the qualified group stage. In May, lifestyle social media platform RedNote purchased its first FIFA broadcast and short-video making rights licensed by China Central Television (CCTV), the country's exclusive live broadcaster for the World Cup. In June, adidas extended its immersive concept sites for Backyard Legends, a video shot for the FIFA World Cup 2026, to Shanghai's Xintiandi, for brand and FIFA promotion. Chinese sponsors like tech firm Hisense, dairy maker Mengniu and toy maker Pop Mart had an on-site presence at the World Cup. Experts said as a game that reaches three quarters of the global population, the soccer World Cup presents a good platform for sponsors to gain popularity, particularly among the young.

title: Humanity Needs to Adapt to Extreme Weather
subtitle: China Economic Weekly July 15, 2026
paragraphs: After a series of heatwaves, typhoons, torrential rains and floods, humanity is enduring much more frequent weather disasters. Since 2020, extreme weather and natural disasters have caused global losses of US$3.6 trillion. To address extreme weather, such as Typhoon Maysak, which drenched Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region and Hubei Province in July, China called for concerted efforts nationwide to offset climate impacts, from preventive measures to evacuations. Meanwhile, with weather satellite forecasts and relief deliveries by drone, tech is playing an essential role in emergency preparedness and rescue. China is also rehabilitating ecosystems, developing flood retention capacities and publicizing survival skills to mitigate disastrous consequences. Experts suggest the world pay much more attention to climate change, otherwise drought and rainstorms will continue to exacerbate.

title: EU Swings Between Carbon Market: Tariffs, Cooperation
subtitle: World Affairs | June 16, 2026
paragraphs: On January 1, the European Union kicked off its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a carbon tariff system involving steel, cement, electricity, aluminum, fertilizers and hydrogen imports. The scheme levies taxes for embedded emissions in accordance with auction prices under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) allowances. As the world's first transnational carbon market set up in 2005, the EU ETS has developed a flexible mechanism of carbon allowances levied on a growing number of industries. China's Ministry of Commerce said the CBAM is an unfair and discriminatory treatment which ignores the country's green contributions. On May 7, China, the EU and Brazil launched the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Market, the world's first carbon-pricing cooperation initiative between developed and developing economies. Experts said the EU's swings between tariffs and cooperation reflect the changing landscape of international trade and investment resulting from geopolitical games.

title: Young Chinese Increase Incomes: Through Side Gigs
subtitle: South Reviews | July 13, 2026
paragraphs: Profiting from professional skills or hobbies, young Chinese people are no longer satisfied with their regular salary. They make handicrafts, tutor or design video games as side gigs, not only to increase their income, but also to expand their abilities beyond the workplace. Considering the high costs and few opportunities in big cities, many youngsters run businesses in smaller cities where costs are lower if they should fail. With increased use of AI, some run small companies to provide tech-centered products such as programs for athlete trackers or navigational aids. By 2021, the gig economy employed 200 million people, about one-seventh of the population. This figure is expected to double by 2036. Amid the growing trend, experts said that whatever the type of employment, dedication is a prerequisite for success.

title: VERBATIM
paragraphs: "How does one explain China's competitiveness then? The answer does not lie in a single policy, but rather in the interaction of industrial organization, human capital, innovation and market scale. China now contains multiple stages of industrial development within one national market. Frontier metropolitan areas coexist with vast manufacturing networks, which creates an internal ‘flying geese' structure, moving some production to lower-cost inland regions, that spans much of the industrial value chain. Products can be designed, tested, manufactured and commercialized within a single integrated ecosystem before being deployed across a market of more than 1.4 billion people."

Guo Kai, executive president of the China Finance 40 Forum (CF40) Research Institute, arguing against a June report from the OECD claiming that China's competitiveness relies on government subsidies, in an article published on opinion piece website Project Syndicate on July 17
"Building AI models requires a long-term mindset and the ability to delay gratification, rather than using others' outputs for temporary gains in the leaderboards."
Zhang Yiming, founder of ByteDance, who said at an internal meeting in August that he would not regard distillation as a shortcut to improve AI models

"As a tool of governance, law may face competition [from new technologies], but the core capabilities of legal professionals cannot be replicated by technology. Code can solve technical problems, but it cannot address questions of legitimacy, fairness and justice. Legal professionals can make value judgments and balance interests. They also can construct rules and think in terms of long-term governance, as well as a commitment to humanistic care and protecting rights. These are boundaries that algorithms cannot cross. In this sense, the AI era does not diminish the importance of law. It instead gives law an even more important mission."
Zhang Linghan, dean of the Institute of Artificial Intelligence Law at China University of Political Science and Law, in a interview with news portal The Paper in late July

"AI outperforms humans when it comes to the left-brain but it has yet to develop the rightbrain, qualities that include empathy, aesthetics and long-term vision. This is where humans have an advantage over AI, and it has nothing to do with data."

Lee Kai-Fu, founder and CEO of Beijing-based Zero One All Things Technology, at an event promoting his new book AI: The Future Has Come at Peking University's National School of Development on August 7

In other words, only when a common external threat emerges will the US set aside competition. But I believe the common challenges humanity faces today, such as climate change, energy crises and public health risks, are that ‘asteroid.' These global issues are far more urgent than competition Professor Wang Fan, deputy director of the Chinese Association of American Studies, at a July forum on area studies and global leadership hosted by the Institute of Area Studies (Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies) and the School of Global Leadership
at the Renmin University of China in Beijing

"Every era has its own icons. Seeing the Forbes List rankings change neither surprises or excites me. It only makes me more vigilant. Wang Jianlin was once the icon of his era, just as I was once a young man whom everyone doubted. The cruelest part of change is that those at the top are always the last to notice it."

Justin Sun, founder of blockchain platform TRON and a prominent figure in cryptocurrency born in the 1990s, responding on X to news that he surpassed Chinese real estate mogul Wang Jianlin on the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List on August 6, with an estimated net worth of US$8.5 billion

"Domestic animation featuring myths is now enjoying a creative boom. Animators have broken free from the stereotype that China's animation industry is still immature and have gained the ability to engage in international cultural expression. At the same time, they face fierce market competition and remain overly reliant on a small number of star IPs. While delivering stunning visual spectacles, they have yet to deepen their thematic expression. They still need to find their way out of the confused and drifting ‘Odyssey phase' and reach the ideal land of artistic expression."
Chang Fangzhou, associate researcher at the Institute of Literature, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, writing for The Paper's Shanghai Arts column in late July

I believe one key reason is that our scientists still lack a sufficiently deep grounding in the humanities, so they have yet to fully appreciate or be deeply inspired by the truth and beauty of nature."
Renowned mathematician Shing-Tung Yau writing in the Party journal Qiushi on August 1

title: Renewable Energy Focus of Ambitious Green Development Roadmap
paragraphs: China has unveiled an ambitious plan for renewable energy and green tech development for the next five years, aimed at tackling carbon emissions while continuing to grow the economy.

The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the National Energy Administration (NEA) released the 15th Five-Year Plan for Renewable Energy Development on July 23, outlining a green energy blueprint from 2026 to 2030.

The plan sets systematic, quantifiable development targets covering total energy consumption, power generation, non-electric utilization and reliable grid substitution. By 2030, China's total renewable energy consumption is expected to hit about 1.8 billion tons of standard coal. Total installed capacity of renewable energy power will reach around 3.5 billion kilowatts, with an annual power output hitting 6 trillion kilowatt-hours. Installed capacity of wind and solar power is planned to surpass 2.8 billion kilowatts, which will account for more than 50 percent of national power capacity. Their combined annual power generation is set to exceed 4 trillion kilowatt-hours accounting for 30 percent of the country's total.

The plan highlights innovative reliable substitution mechanisms to address the intermittency of wind and solar resources. By 2030, wind and solar power installations equipped with energy storage should deliver average firm capacity equivalent to 8 percent of installed capacity at peak electricity demand periods. During summer and winter night peaks, wind and solar power is expected to contribute over 20 percent of grid supply. Over the 2026- 2030 period, China will add more than 300 gigawatts of reliable renewable peak-generation capacity.

The plan proposes to expand nonelectric applications for renewable energy. By 2030, the scale of non-power renewable energy utilization is expected to grow 1.5 times compared with 2025 levels, with renewable hydrogen production reaching 2 million tons annually.

To realize those targets, China will continue to construct large-scale wind and solar bases in desert and Gobi regions, planning to increase installed wind and solar capacity in northwestern, northeastern and northern regions by at least 370 million kilowatts. Offshore wind will be boosted in coastal areas, with cumulative installed capacity increasing by 100 million kilowatts by 2030. The country will also encourage other green energy, improve new energy storage systems, optimize grid connection mechanisms, and coordinate resource development, grid transmission and market consumption.

Two months before the new plan was issued, the NDRC and NEA published a document on implementing compulsory consumption of renewable energy which will take effect as of August 1. An NEA official told media that the compulsory consumption target will encourage key industries to use more renewable energy, advance the green energy market and optimize the distribution of green energy resources across the country.

According to the NEA's latest data, by the end of June 2026, China's total installed capacity of renewable energy reached 2.455 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of the country's total power capacity. In the first half of 2026, newly added renewable energy capacity stood at 117 million kilowatts, accounting for 73.9 percent of all newly built power installations. In the same period, China's renewable energy generated nearly 2 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity, 9 percent growth year-onyear, accounting for 41.2 percent of total electricity generation.

On July 30, the NEA published its China New-type Energy Storage Development Report, which said that during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), the new-type energy storage industry has shifted from the preliminary commercial application stage to a new phase of scaled-up development, with installed capacity soaring from 3 million kilowatts to 136 million kilowatts.

Experts said the new plan upgrades China's renewable energy strategy from large-scale expansion to high-quality growth which prioritizes stability, efficiency and system integration over sheer capacity growth. It will also consolidate China's leading role in the global renewable energy industry and drive global green and low-carbon cooperation.

title: UNESCO Recognizes Jingdezhen Porcelain Heritage
paragraphs: China's Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List at the 48th World Heritage Committee meeting held in Busan, South Korea on July 25.

Located in northeastern Jiangxi Province, the Jingdezhen heritage site, 7,524.7 hectares in total, consists of five main clusters, 15 constituent components and 45 heritage spots that reflect the entire production cycle, including porcelain production sites, mine sites and material sites. They formed a complete porcelain industrial system for 900 years from the 10th to 19th century.

The UNESCO committee praised Jingdezhen's authenticity and integrity, recognizing its innovative integration with global porcelain-making techniques and arts. It is the world's first heritage site that is themed around porcelain production, and marks the international acknowledgement of Jingdezhen's millennium-old craft and its historic role in cross-cultural exchanges.
The latest inscription lifts the number of world heritage entries in China to 61.

title: China Rolls Out Security: Probe into Imported: Printers and Copiers
paragraphs: China's Ministry of Commerce on August 5 announced the country's inaugural national security investigation in the foreign trade arena, targeting imported office equipment with printing and copying functions that feature foreign system software.
The investigation will pay special attention to foreign system software that covers driver software and embedded software developed, tested or maintained by foreign individuals or entities.

Investigators will weigh the national security risks by inspecting the impact of imported products, technologies or services, domestic demand and the extent of reliance on foreign imports, as well as the competitiveness of local office equipment manufacturers and their ability to meet local demand.

The investigation will also examine the impact of relevant foreign government policies and measures on China's national security interests, as well as any other matters affecting national security interests in foreign trade.
A spokesperson with the Ministry of Commerce said the inquiry will abide by legal procedures and protect the lawful interests of all involved stakeholders.
The investigation is to be completed within 12 months of the date of the announcement.

title: Chinese Scientists Create Precision Map of Moon's Geology
paragraphs: Chinese scientists have completed a 1:5,000,000 global lunar geological map, accompanied by partial geological maps of the Moon's north and south polar regions.

The map's author, the Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, told the Xinhua News Agency that the map, 280 centimeters long and 120 centimeters high, precisely identifies 13,519 impact craters and 81 impact basins across the lunar surface. It also categorizes lunar geological features into 14 types of geological structure and 17 rock types.

Analyzing recent research, Chinese scientists confirmed evidence of volcanic eruptions on the moon as late as 2 billion years ago, extending the known active volcanic history of the satellite by a billion years. Researchers have re-ordered the late-stage geological history of the moon and established an updated lunar chronological table.

China launched the Chang'e-6 lunar probe on May 3, 2024 which successfully returned to Earth with 1,935.3 grams of lunar soil samples from the far side of the moon 53 days later. The same year, China released the world's first 1:2,500,000 lunar geological map. The Chang'e-7 lunar probe is scheduled to launch in the latter half of 2026 to explore the moon's south polar region.

title: Tourism Platform Ctrip: Hit with Heavy Anti-: Monopoly Fine
paragraphs: China's

State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) on July 25 issued a major anti-monopoly administrative penalty against Ctrip, a leading Chinese tourism booking platform, with combined fines and confiscated illegal gains hitting 5.179 billion yuan (US$739.9m).

Based on China's Anti-Monopoly Law, the fine includes confiscated unlawful earnings of 1.658 billion yuan (US$236.9m) and an additional fine of 3.521 billion yuan (US$503m). Authorities also ordered the tourism platform to return 122 million yuan (US$17.4m) of compulsory order deposits to hotel operators. The penalty equals 7.5 percent of Ctrip's domestic sales revenue in 2025.

The SAMR said that Ctrip abused its dominant standing in the domestic online accommodation booking market by forcing some providers to enter into exclusive deals with it and forcing some hotels to give it the lowest prices among competing platforms. Those practices have broken fair market competition, hurt hotel operators and consumers' rights and interest, and obstructed the healthy development of the industry.
Ctrip stated that it would accept the verdict and carry out comprehensive public rectification.

title: APEC Data Meeting Releases Statement on Cooperation, Innovation
paragraphs: The 2026 APEC Data for Growth High- Level Roundtable was held in Chengdu, Sichuan Province on July 25, where member economies reached a consensus that data has become a new engine for economic growth.
As a core event of APEC Digital Week 2026, the meeting hosted in-depth exchanges over unlocking data value, technological innovation and regional productivity improvement.

In closed-door discussions, participants finalized the APEC Data for Growth High- Level Roundtable Chair's Statement which defines three directions for data cooperation, including fostering an open and enabling environment for data access and use, strengthening data-driven innovation and application, and deepening cooperation on data connectivity.

Liu Liehong, director of China's National Data Administration, said the statement shows that APEC's data dialogue has shifted from "managing data to using data," stressing that data-related cooperation among APEC member economies offers vast market opportunities and huge growth potentials that will open new paths for inclusive growth and shared prosperity.
The latest data from China's National Data Administration showed that China generated 52.26 zettabytes of data in 2025, a 27.28 percent growth year-on-year.

title: Wang Hong
paragraphs: On July 23, Chinese mathematician Wang Hong, 35, was awarded the Fields Medal at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, US. Wang and fellow Chinese mathematician Deng Yu, 37, were among four mathematicians to receive the medal, widely regarded as the most prestigious award in mathematics.

Wang is the first Chinese woman to win the prize. The award recognizes her work in solving the century-old three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, a longstanding open problem at the intersection of analysis and geometry.

Wang was born in 1991 in Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Her parents were local middle school teachers, and her father taught mathematics. She was admitted to the Department of Geophysics at Peking University (PKU) at the age of 16. A year later, she switched her major to mathematics and earned her bachelor's degree from PKU in 2011. She then continued her studies in mathematics, earning a master's degree from École Polytechnique in France.

Wang later moved to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she specialized in Fourier analysis and geometric measure theory and earned her PhD in 2019. She is now an associate professor at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences.

After receiving the Fields Medal, Wang quickly became a household name on Chinese social media. Some netizens, however, drew attention to her luxury accessories, including a Cartier necklace and ring, and speculated that her annual income could reach 3-4 million yuan (US$445,000-593,000). The remarks sparked criticism from some who questioned whether a prominent academic should be so interested in luxury goods and material wealth.

The debate reflects a longstanding expectation in Chinese society that academic researchers should be indifferent to fame and fortune and willing to live modestly, as if material pursuits were inherently at odds with the pursuit of knowledge.

Others pushed back against the criticism, arguing that scientific achievement does not require poverty and that Wang has every right to enjoy the rewards of her work. Many said that using one's talent to build a successful life with dignity is entirely compatible with being a researcher today.
Why Hyrox is taking off among young Chinese

Hyrox, a hybrid fitness race combining running and functional workouts, has surged in popularity among young Chinese this summer, boosting interest in a new form of competitive fitness akin to CrossFit.

Originating in Germany in 2017, Hyrox combines an eight-kilometer run with eight types of workouts, including sled pushes, sled pulls and medicine-ball work. It entered the Chinese market two years ago and has taken the country's fitness community by storm this year.

More than 10,000 people participated in a Hyrox race in Shanghai in May. According to Yuan Fang, head of Hyrox China, Hyrox has established long-term partnerships with more than 600 gyms across major Chinese cities. On Chinese lifestyle platform RedNote, the Hyrox hashtag has more than 130 million views.
Hyrox China participants are a clearly defined group, Yuan told the Chengdu Daily. Most are aged 25 to 40 and work in industries including finance and tech.

"Traditional fitness lacks a standardized competitive format. Hyrox fills that gap with a clear, universal set of rules, and that gives people a tangible way to track their progress and push their own limits," Yuan said.

title: Birdwatching Economy: Nest Eggs
paragraphs: uang Zhiqiang scoops a handful
of
mealworms
from a plastic bucket and walks toward a bird hide. Placing the worms into grooves on bamboo poles above a man-made pond, he blows a whistle. Before long, a variety of wild birds appear.

A chestnut-capped babbler was the first to land. It ate cautiously, and soon flew away. Next came a red-whiskered bulbul, which landed with bright chirps, yet took flight after only a few pecks, yielding its spot to a pair of shamas.

"The chestnut-capped babbler is extremely timid. Locals here in Guangxi traditionally call it the ‘ghost bird.' It has a beautiful song, but you can hardly ever spot it. Chestnut-capped babblers are intimidated by red-whiskered bulbuls, so they fly off as soon as bulbuls turn up. When shamas arrive, especially male shamas, the bulbuls get scared, as shamas are far more aggressive," Huang said, sitting in a hide five meters from the pond.

Huang, 43, has become an expert on bird behavior. He lives in Nonggang Village in the karst landscapes of southwest Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Famous among ornithologists and birders worldwide as the site where the Nonggang babbler, a bird endemic to China, was first identified, the village and nearby nature reserve is a soughtafter birdwatching destination. Most Hvillagers have benefited from birdwatching tourism, building ponds and hides among farmlands and woodlands. Huang is among some 40 local professional guides.

In spring and summer, there is abundant natural food, so wild birds do not require supplementary feeding. Even so, Huang often rides his electric scooter to his bird pond. Sometimes he sits quietly in a chair, occasionally putting out a handful of feed and blowing his whistle. "I just want to see whether the birds will come and what time they arrive."
Apart from common resident species, Huang's pond is known for chestnutcapped babblers and yellow-eyed babblers, attracting wildlife photographers between September and March.

Su Shangzhu, Party secretary of Zhubu Township, which administers Nonggang, told NewsChina that the village has laid out more than 30 birdwatching ponds, with 12 trails that cover a range of habitats and species. Ten villages participate in birdwatching tourism, benefiting 344 households with 1,422 residents. Families can earn on average 20,000 yuan (US$3,000) more a year, with some earning more than 100,000 yuan (US$14,800).
Taking Flight

Nonggang's birdwatching boom began with the discovery of a new species. In 2005, ecologist Jiang Aiwu from Guangxi University's College of Forestry and his supervisor, renowned ornithologist Zhou Fang, found an unknown babbler population in the seasonal rainforest of Nonggang National Nature Reserve. Formally documented and named the Nonggang babbler (Stachyris nonggangensis), it is one of the rare bird species independently discovered, described and named by Chinese ornithologists after 1949.

Located in southwest Guangxi and established in 1979, Nonggang National Nature Reserve covers over 10,000 hectares. It is China's sole protected zone dedicated to seasonal rainforests in its northern tropical limestone region, sheltering rare flora and fauna including white-headed langurs, François' langurs, Nonggang babblers, Parashorea chinensis, an endangered evergreen tree, cycads and golden camellias.

Researchers have recorded vascular plant species and 429 vertebrates, including 66 mammals, 66 reptiles, 31 amphibians and 266 birds, accounting for 36 percent of Guangxi's total bird species. "Out of the 266 documented bird species, only dozens appear regularly. About 10 are really sought-after by birders," Nong Zhengquan, chief of the reserve's Forestry Administration and Resources Protection Section, told NewsChina in early July.

Jiang noted that the Zhuang ethnic group who live in the area possess knowledge that was crucial to finding the Nonggang babbler, and often had their own names for species. "Rangers shared bird descriptions with me - for example, a curved-beaked bird that spends most of its time on the ground,' he said. Nong Weihong, a former ranger, pioneer bird guide and founder of Nonggang's first birdwatching homestay, spoke of a species called "swing bird," named for its hanging treetop nests, which Jiang later identified as the long-tailed broadbill.

After Jiang's research confirmed Nonggang babblers lived in and around Nonggang Reserve, birders from home and abroad flocked there. It led to the development of community-led birdwatching tourism outside the reserve's boundaries.

"Liuzhou Birdwatching Society from Guangxi was crucial in the industry's early phase. I first took its members into mountains searching for the Nonggang babbler. Recognizing Nonggang's birdwatching potential, they backed Nong Weihong to convert buildings into visitor accommodation," Jiang said. Around 2015, farmers began building artificial feeding ponds to attract wild birds.

"Nong Weihong created photography hides using kapok blossoms and mealworms. Photographers paid around 80 yuan (US$11.8) each. A single hide could hold over a dozen people, generating steady daily revenue." Jiang said birdwatching has lifted incomes and boosted wildlife conservation awareness. He never anticipated discovering a new bird would transform livelihoods in this remote mountain region.

News of the Nonggang babbler rippled across the global birdwatching community. Visitors soon discovered other targets: the Indochinese green magpie, brown-breasted hill partridge, white-browed piculet, blue-backed pitta and long-tailed broadbill.

Huang Zhiqiang started working as a guide around 2008. Before that, his family earned 30,000 yuan (US$4,443) annually growing sugarcane. "I knew nothing about birds. I learned from training sessions hosted by the township government and nature reserve, featuring lectures from invited experts."

Today he runs Nonggang Bird Lodge, a three-story homestay completed in 2014, which can host 30 guests. Birdwatching has two peak seasons: late September to March for pond photography, and April to late June for the breeding season, ideal for nest shots. During these seasons, Nonggang's 15 homestays are usually fully booked.
Huang Haipeng used to work in neighboring
Guangdong

Province. Lured by birdwatching opportunities, he returned home around 2014 to become a bird guide. After years of accumulating capital, he invested 800,000 yuan (US$118,500) to open Xiaopeng Inn in 2022. The inn has 14 rooms, and his family manages two ponds known for Indochinese green magpie sightings.

According to Huang Haipeng, combined revenue from homestays, photography hides, transport and guiding brings his family at least 100,000 yuan (US$14,800) annually, far more than his salary in Guangdong.

Local communities have formed clear systems for labor division and profit sharing. Homestay operators provide lodging, meals and transport, while revenue from photography hides belongs to pond owners. During breeding season, if stable nesting sites are located, photography fees are paid to the pond owner who first found the nest.
Beak Practice
Villagers once relied on mountain resources for survival, with hunting and trapping wild birds long entrenched. Poaching created sharp friction between villagers and staff in Nonggang Reserve.
Zhao Wenqing, president of Longzhou Birdwatching Society, said the illegal trade in wild birds was rife in the 1980s and 90s, driving some species almost to extinction.

In the 1980s to 1990s when the nature reserve was newly set up, household income was low, and some felled trees illegally. "Whenever our staff halted such illegal activities by law, villagers grew resentful. Many believed conservation undermined their livelihoods and resisted our work. This rift persisted for years and proved extremely difficult to resolve," Nong Zhengquan said.

The arrival of birdwatching ecotourism helped villagers recognize wild birds' long-term value, and they began protecting birds, enabling gradual population recovery. Former bird trappers became professional guides, homestay operators and eco-tourism service providers.

The reserve, in partnership with Longzhou Birdwatching Society, helped villagers design nature trails, build ponds and set prices. The economic benefits they derive encourage them to safeguard forests and prevent logging and poaching, as well as boost conservation cooperation between communities and wildlife officials.
Nong Zhengquan emphasized that the selection of viewing sites must be based on species' natural behaviors.

"Reserve researchers conduct longterm bird surveys to map activity zones, while villagers observe wildlife yearround in the mountains. We combine both datasets to select suitable locations. Observation sites and targeted luring activities are only approved once we confirm regular presence of [certain] species," he said.
But, he added, attracting birds through artificial means is controversial, as feeding and photography can disturb birds.

"For this reason, authorities have introduced formal regulations. Approval for nest photography requires on-site assessment led by Longzhou Birdwatching Society, weighing risks such as nest abandonment or disturbance to fledglings," he said.

This means hides are not close to nests and are rotated every year, with no activity allowed around nest building and hatching. "Everyone understands persistent disruption can drive parent birds to abandon nests, eliminating future observation opportunities," Nong said.
Nonggang's
birdwatching

sector relies on coordinated support from local government, the nature reserve, research institutions and civic stakeholders. In the beginning there were steep obstacles, such as rudimentary infrastructure, poor accessibility and inadequate sanitation, with no previous foundation for the niche sector.

The reserve and local administrators held discussions in villages to identify priorities. The roadmap they developed called to upgrade basic infrastructure first before making quality improvements. Road surfacing, power grid renovation and full network coverage topped the agenda, while parking, vocational training and village beautification were longer term goals. As more villagers joined in planning and governance, money was allocated to deliver the projects.

From 2017 to 2019, Longzhou County invested over 20 million yuan (US$2.96m) in infrastructure upgrades, including paved roads, kitchen and toilet renovations, drainage systems and parking lots. Guangxi's first dedicated birdwatching hub, Nonggang Ecological Birdwatching Popular Science Base, was launched.

Villagers were the prime beneficiaries, with better living conditions and more income streams. Some built bird ponds and homestays, while others offer tourist shuttles and photography support. Nearly every household has one or two members working in birdwatching tourism.

The reserve directed funding into vocational training for bird guiding, botanical outreach, amphibian and reptile observation, nature journaling, wildlife photography and catering. More than 100 people, mostly young and returning migrants, participated. Officials visited other birdwatching hubs to observe best practices.
Pecking Order

In some parts of China, unregulated expansion of bird ponds has triggered overbuilding, homogenous offerings and cutthroat competition. While individual ponds create limited ecological disruption, concentrated unplanned development accumulates environmental pressure. Uneven profit distribution has sparked internal conflicts. Excluded villagers have damaged facilities and disrupted operations, pushing promising eco-industries toward collapse.

"In the early phase, we shared negative cases of poorly managed birdwatching industries with local stakeholders, repeatedly urging Longzhou to avoid malpractice like unethical bird luring for photos, ruinous price wars, habitat damage through arbitrary tree trimming, and conflicts over exclusive photography spots," Zhong Jia, honorary chairperson of the China Birdwatching Network Alliance, told NewsChina.
County and township governments carried out door-to-door outreach, hosted forums bringing together academics, officials and villagers, and rolled out multi-level management regulations.

"A viable replicable birdwatching economy requires inclusive benefitsharing and institutional governance. If only a small group profits from natural resources, impressive short-term gains do not amount to a successful development model," Zhong emphasized.

Zhao Wenqing said there is one inviolable rule for photography management: human activity must never disrupt animals' natural behavior. "We do sustained early-stage monitoring to evaluate risks of breeding disturbance and strictly ban trimming vegetation around nests. Any guide altering habitats against regulations will have the site suspended," he said.

A widely accepted set of norms has taken root locally. Whoever discovers a bird nest holds priority to operate the site and earn associated revenue. Simple photography hides require minimal investment, roughly 100-200 yuan (US$15-30) for ground levelling and shade netting.

Globally, supplementary feeding at bird ponds remains controversial. Longterm artificial provision of food may alter avian migration and breeding cycles, shift interspecies competition and increase bird aggregation, raising risks of pathogen transmission.

Professor Jiang Aiwu takes a nuanced stance on bird-pond feeding. "Supplementary feeding in Nonggang mainly runs in the October to February dry season when food and water is scarce. During breeding seasons, birds rarely rely on artificial supplies and retain wild foraging skills. Fixed feeding reduces starvation risks in dry months, with only small periodic portions provided. In addition, visiting birds are not permanent groups, so dependency does not develop," Jiang said.

"There are risks, as permanent feeding spots attract predators such as snakes and raptors. Overall, Nonggang's bird pond model delivers net benefits under current conditions, though consistent standardized management is critical."

Jiang told NewsChina his research team has long monitored the ecological effects of bird ponds and nest photography, sharing data with authorities to advance sustainable industry growth. Long-term monitoring shows Nonggang babbler numbers within the reserve are rising.

Zhao Wenqing regularly leads nationwide birdwatching groups to Nonggang. Before visitors arrive, guides design detailed photography schedules based on recent bird activity data. The itineraries target five to six key species through morning, midday and afternoon sites. The focus now is mostly on spring tours.

"Spring coincides with resident birds' breeding season and migratory bird passage, lifting overall sighting diversity. We've extended routes to Mount Daqing on the China-Vietnam border, Longzhou's highest terrain, offering sightings of migrants and unique highland species," Zhao said.

Li Weidong, a 55-year-old bridge engineer and wildlife photographer from Kunming, Yunnan Province, has visited Nonggang four times. "I've traveled to major bird pond photography sites nationwide, most showing obvious signs of heavy human intervention. Nonggang preserves far more natural habitats, and I consider its birdwatching experience among China's finest," he said.
Guangxi
birdwatcher
Lai

Liping visited Nonggang in June, and told NewsChina she was impressed with the local guides' knowledge. "They know exactly when birds leave nests to feed chicks, feeding frequencies, primary prey and feeding intervals. delivering an excellent visitor experience," Lai said, adding that accommodation and guiding prices are reasonable."
Sky's the Limit

Across China's karst birdwatching destinations, Nonggang ranks among the finest. Most established birdwatching areas lie in Yunnan, which rely on year-round fixed bird ponds. Nonggang pioneered regulated breeding-season nest photography in China.

Bird pond visits run September to March, leaving villagers with an offseason income gap. Launched in 2019, nest photography fills the March-June void and delivers year-round earnings. They are developing nature education programs like night birdwatching and insect observation to cover July through September. But most remain small-scale initiatives organized by conservation volunteers, and there are no partnerships with big travel agencies.

Nonggang Village employs 25 fulltime professional bird guides, alongside seasonal amateur guides such as villagers who discover wild bird nests. While the discoverer manages the site, Longzhou Birdwatching Society specialists monitor it to avoid disrupting incubation.

Nong Qijian, 58, located a redheaded trogon nest in May and built a basic viewing hide. He usually hosts over a dozen photographers daily, but only earned 1,000 yuan (US$148) that breeding season, as trogon chicks fledge in 10 days. Some nests are in difficult terrain, so casual guides face highly unstable incomes.
Nong
Qijian's
annual

household income is around 50,000 yuan (US$7,400), putting his family in the village's lower-middle income tier, but it is not enough to build his own homestay, although there is demand for more lodging.

Jiang Aiwu believes in making sure the whole community benefits. At present, homestay owners and bird guides receive most birdwatching revenue, excluding other villagers, who do not make enough from regular agriculture. He favors Yunnan's collective template where village communities share the benefits, while some skilled operators can earn more.

Visitor Lai Liping feels positive about Nonggang's development path: "The bird pond model suppresses bird trapping and the wildlife trade, allowing villagers to profit sustainably from conservation. I hope the model can be replicated to encourage broader wild bird protection."

title: Birdwatching Economy: Flight Paths
paragraphs: Yunnan Province hosts China's richest bird habitats and avian diversity. Nearly 40 percent of China's over 250 birdwatching sites lie in Yunnan, making it a leader in the burgeoning industry.

Through managing artificial bird ponds, resource sharing and local wisdom, its model has given mountain villagers who once hunted birds the chance to become wildlife guardians, creating an eco-friendly sector driven by community.

Wu Fei is a long-standing expert on avian ecology. An associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences Kunming Institute of Zoology, he is spearheading the introduction of the nation's first provincial-level birdwatching standards.
In our exclusive interview, Wu shared his thoughts on the opportunities, risks and long-term outlook for birdwatching, and what that means for the future of eco-tourism.
NewsChina: What impact has the boom in birdwatching brought to wildlife habitats and rural communities?

Wu Fei: In recent years, birdwatching has grown quickly in China and attracted more people across the country. But overall, the sector is still in its early stages, developing mainly through spontaneous local efforts. Unified industry standards and top-level overall planning are still absent, yet the overall industrial foundation has been firmly established.

Survey data shows that the number of bird pond sites nationwide exceeded 250 several years ago and it continues to expand. Thanks to its unique ecological endowments and abundant bird resources, Yunnan has the most concentrated bird resources and the most mature birdwatching industry in China.

As a distinctive eco-industry, birdwatching has shown that conservation and rural development can go hand in hand. In the past, wild birds were an important protein source for ethnic communities in the remote mountains of Yunnan. Today, businesses including bird pond operation, bird guiding, rural homestays and catering services provide villagers with stable and sustainable sources of income.

The industry has fundamentally transformed local people's awareness and livelihoods. Former bird hunters have turned into active forest and habitat guardians, voluntarily protecting wild birds. The substantial improvement in villagers' conservation awareness has greatly reduced pressures on nature reserves and strengthened grassroots ecological conservation.

In villages such as the mountainous Baihualing in the city of Baoshan and Shiti in Yingjiang County, Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, the six-month birdwatching peak season alone generates considerable household incomes. Meanwhile, it drives supporting industries including produce sales and transportation, equipment maintenance and nature education, enabling the whole village to share in the dividends of ecological resources.

The bird pond model provides an innovative solution to the dilemma of ecological protection and economic development in remote mountain areas. It effectively helped villagers lift themselves from impoverishment during China's poverty alleviation campaign. Now, its eco-friendly and people-centered approach pairs with China's rural revitalization strategy.

Practice has proven that the bird pond model forms a sustainable green development system. It activates the ecological value of rural resources, boosts rural revitalization and continuously safeguards regional biodiversity, organically integrating ecological protection, livelihood improvement and rural development.
NC: Some worry that bird ponds and supplementary feeding could harm wild bird populations. Are those concerns justified?

WF: Public anxiety over bird ponds largely centers on risks associated with supplementary feeding. Critics fear constant provision of food will modify wild birds' instinctive behavior, foster food dependency and disrupt natural population cycles. But research conducted at birdwatching ponds in Yunnan shows the adverse effects of properly managed artificial feeding are relatively minor and controllable.
Yunnan has dry and wet seasons. Most bird ponds follow a six-month open,
six-month
closed

schedule. Between October-November and April- May, the dry season creates water and wild food shortages. Bird ponds supply water and moderate supplementary feed to offset these deficits. All feeding stops from late May to late September during the wet season, pushing birds back to full natural foraging. Temporary behavioral changes caused by human activity gradually subside.

Seasonal supplementary feeding in Yunnan is similar in some ways to established practices in other countries, such as backyard bird feeding. In both cases, people provide food to birds to attract them for greater birdwatching opportunities. However, feeding at bird ponds is typically seasonal and is combined with measures like replenishing water, providing concealed viewing areas and following standardized management. This makes it quite different from backyard bird feeding, which is often year-round. Research suggests that carefully controlling the amount of food provided and how feeding is managed can help prevent birds from becoming over-reliant on artificial food sources. So far, no evidence has been found that moderate supplemental feeding leads to significant changes in bird community structure.

Baihualing, a well-established site, hosts just over 20 bird ponds with tightly controlled scale. Long-term monitoring detects no significant shifts in either the species richness or community composition of local bird populations.

We've documented positive outcomes for multiple nationally protected pheasants such as the grey peacock-pheasant and Kalij pheasant. Notably, the Class I protected grey peacock-pheasant has seen considerable population growth, with no detectable disruption to its habitat selection or breeding caused by bird ponds. In summary, standardized bird ponds improve breeding output among medium and large wild pheasants and help populations of threatened avian species recover. The model serves as a viable solution for Southwest China's mountain landscapes.
NC: Baihualing and Shiti are often cited as successful examples of birdwatching-driven
rural
development. What makes their model work, and what should other regions avoid when trying to replicate it?
WF: The villages' sustained growth hinges on community-led governance with
co-development
and
shared benefits.

Both communities endured chaotic unregulated early development. Initially, a handful of villagers controlled bird pond resources and captured most of the profits, shutting out the majority. Widening inequality sparked frequent conflicts over resources.

Locals came to recognize birds depend on whole forest ecosystems rather than separate ponds. Profit concentration among a few was unsustainable and risked retaliatory ecological damage. Through self-governance, they built a collective revenue-sharing framework.

Bird pond operators now allocate part of their earnings to a communal ecological fund. The fund covers village infrastructure upkeep, forest management, sanitation and unified ticketing. Year-end surpluses are divided equally among all villagers. This multi-stakeholder system stabilizes the industry. Operators retain viable profits, while other residents earn money through bird guiding, transport, homestays, catering and selling local goods. Even local non-participants receive annual ecological dividends, further reducing disputes.

Yunnan's ethnic villages have tight kinship networks and a strong collective consciousness that aid in sharing benefits. The model has attracted delegations from other provinces in China to visit and study it, hoping to draw inspiration from it.

But two key principles must be followed to replicate it successfully. First, local villagers must have the leading role and outside capital cannot monopolize the space. The birdwatching economy is a niche eco-industry reliant on intact natural habitats. Large external investment, over-commercialization and drastic changes to the landscape harm native ecosystems, crowd out local livelihoods, fuel social friction and betray the goal of ecologically driven rural prosperity.

Second, policies and distribution rules must be tailor-made. Regions vary widely in customs, demographics, development foundations and public expectations. Enforcing uniform formulas could trigger new village tensions. A reasonable income distribution system is also vital. Excessive wealth gaps between bird pond operators and other villagers could breed resentment and destabilize communities.

Nationwide, the birdwatching industry remains exploratory and lacks unified national top-down rules. Its strength lies in flexible grassroots governance. Given China's vast regional diversity, any national standards will require local adjustment. The benchmark for assessing rural industrial models is institutional fairness and public acceptance, alongside tangible ecological and livelihood gains, rather than rigid rules and regulations.

The broader industry rejects compulsory standardized pricing, revenue allocation and operating rules. Respecting organic, locally evolved practices aligns with industrial realities. Local governments and nature reserves fulfill supportive, supervisory and guiding functions while preserving room for grassroots innovation.
NC: What role does local ecological knowledge passed down through generations play in the birdwatching industry?

WF: Communities that have lived in these mountains for centuries have inherited a complete set of indigenous ecological wisdom forged through generations of coexistence with nature. They know exactly which tree species each bird favors, their seasonal activity ranges and hidden roosting spots. This intuitive, place-based knowledge cannot be quickly acquired by outside researchers and bird enthusiasts, and makes up the core competitiveness of local bird guides.

Nevertheless, this valuable traditional knowledge has yet to be systematically sorted and cataloged, and there are few dedicated studies measuring its practical value within the birdwatching sector. Going forward, we can standardize the archiving of these ecological insights and integrate them into the full spectrum of wildlife conservation and bird pond management to fully unlock the potential of their experience for the birdwatching economy.
NC: Yunnan is drafting new guidelines for birdwatching activities and bird pond management. What will these standards mean for the industry's future development?
WF: Few rural industries deliver steady, direct income to ordinary villagers in remote mountain regions. The birdwatching economy is emerging as a practical eco-industry based around communities.
Unlike mainstream cultural tourism, the bird pond model creates a distinctive framework where ecological protection, rural income growth and streamlined ecological governance improve together.

But because the sector depends on unique wildlife resources and highquality habitats, unregulated expansion is not conducive to its healthy and sustainable development. To address demand for standardized practices in the industry, Yunnan provincial authorities commissioned me to lead the drafting of provincial birdwatching tourism plans, industry guidelines and construction specifications.
Currently, our team is working to finalize the compilation of the Standards for Bird Pond Construction and the Yunnan Province Guidelines for Birdwatching.

Importantly, the new rules avoid rigid, universal numerical mandates such as fixed feed amounts, uniform pond spacing or set photography distances. Bird behavior shifts with seasons, climate and resource availability, rendering static figures unsuitable for diverse ecosystems. Precise regional quantitative thresholds require further targeted research.

Current regulations center on three core ecological and safety bottom lines. First is facility safety standards. Many Yunnan bird ponds are in remote mountainous areas, with steep terrain, posing certain safety risks. Specifications set requirements for viewing hides, platforms and trails to mitigate fall hazards.

The second is wildfire prevention and sanitation rules. Peak birdwatching time coincides with Yunnan's high-risk dry season. The standards tighten fire control and standardize waste management to safeguard forest ecosystems.

Third comes scientific feeding protocols. Permanent year-round feeding is explicitly banned. Operations should follow seasonal cycles, with supplementary feeding concentrated in dry seasons. Permitted foods include mealworms, grains and fresh fruit matching birds' natural diets. Hazardous feed threatening avian health and ecological balance is prohibited.

The provincial standard establishes a foundational framework. No unified, mature international standards exist for bird pond construction and management. Yunnan's emerging provincial standards will steer orderly development across China and offer actionable local experience for global eco-industry governance.
NC: Birdwatching is highly seasonal. How are communities in Yunnan creating more stable, year-round sources of income?

WF: Seasonal fluctuation is intrinsic to birdwatching. The six-month feeding cycle safeguards the ecology and reduces the likelihood of dependence on supplementary food, so intensive year-round operations are inadvisable. To counter unstable seasonal revenues, established birdwatching villages across Yunnan have adopted integrated "birdwatching plus" models, easing over-reliance on a single sector and boosting off-season earnings.

Three sustainable revenue pillars have emerged. First, nature education and research: Hubs such as Baihualing engage seasoned local bird guides to deliver immersive programs including night insect observation and ornithology outreach. These attract families and student study tours, filling the off-season tourism gap and smoothing annual business volumes. Second, integrated agritourism: Regions around Baoshan have launched distinctive "birdwatching plus coffee" itineraries tied to canopy farming. Local produce and ethnic handicrafts are marketed alongside tourism, converting visitor flows into diversified agricultural income. Third, year-round auxiliary services: Homestays, local catering and short-distance transport operate independently of birdwatching seasons, delivering permanent village employment.

Diversification gradually reduces villagers' over-dependence on bird photography revenue and builds a more robust rural industrial system. In Baihualing, several young residents have returned from cities to run study tour and cultural tourism programs. Still, the number of returnees remains limited. Most are relatives of leading operators. For most villagers, urban employment offers more reliable income than the local birdwatching trade.
NC: Looking ahead, what would an ideal birdwatching industry look like in Yunnan, and what are the biggest challenges to achieving it?

WF: Yunnan hosts over 1,000 bird species, China's richest avian diversity. Its optimal development framework has three pillars. First, streamlined resource management: Authorities should catalogue prefecture-level flagship birds such as green peafowl and great hornbill, document stable viewing periods and create standardized birdwatching route guides to support independent types of visitors.

Second, professional services: Yunnan needs to train local expert bird guides equipped with regional ornithological and conservation knowledge, alongside varied lodging from budget inns to premium eco-homestays, to serve diverse visitors.

Third, coordinated cross-regional development: Following provincial guidelines, interconnected tourism loops with complementary wildlife resources can redistribute visitor traffic across prefectures, uniting avian resources to build nationally famous birdwatching brands.

Major constraints limiting growth exist in physical and service infrastructure. Physically, most bird sites occupy remote mountains with difficult transport. Service-wise, there are no formal training systems for bird guides.

Research on local feeding regimes and carrying capacity (how many visitors a region can support) remains inadequate, while cross-prefecture and interprovincial route coordination progresses need to be strengthened.
NC: As Yunnan develops more highend birdwatching routes, how can it balance tourism, scientific research and wildlife protection?
WF: I believe the key is to build a virtuous cycle where birdwatching tourism, scientific research and wildlife conservation reinforce one another, rather than being treated as competing interests.
First,
high-quality

birdwatching tourism generates direct economic benefits for local communities. This economic incentive naturally raises residents' awareness of conservation. When birds become a sustainable source of income, protecting them becomes a shared community interest rather than an external mandate. At the same time, well-guided birdwatching activities serve as a form of public science education, helping visitors understand the ecological value of these species and fostering a broader culture of conservation.

Second, birdwatchers produce valuable scientific data, such as species distribution records, population trends and seasonal migration patterns. This data often covers large areas over time that professional researchers alone cannot achieve.

Third, research based on this data enables scientists to develop evidencebased conservation strategies, such as identifying priority protection zones, understanding population dynamics or assessing the impacts of environmental changes. More effective conservation leads to healthier bird populations and more diverse species, which makes birdwatching destinations more attractive, drawing more tourists and generating further economic returns.

In this way, tourism fuels conservation motivation, conservation enables scientific data collection, science informs better protection measures and better protection sustains the very resource that makes tourism viable. It is a self-reinforcing loop where each pillar strengthens the others.

title: Youth Football: Lofty Goals
paragraphs: hen 12-year-old Meng Xinyi of Chinese Football Boy (CFB) club stepped up to the penalty spot on June 2, spectators at Rome's La Borghesiana Sports Center held their breath.
A goal would seal the Sigismondi Cup, Italy's premier nine-a-side U12 tournament that sees youth teams from top-flight clubs around the world.

At the referee's whistle, Meng sprinted toward the ball and struck it with the inside of his right foot. The shot curled into the net's top-right corner. Although Everton's youth goalkeeper guessed correctly and stretched to his right, he could only watch the ball fly past him.
The young Chinese players and their supporters erupted in celebration. CFB had defeated the Everton youth team, from Liverpool, UK, 5-4 on penalties. Overcome
with
excitement,
Meng pulled off his jersey and celebrated with a somersault.
Led by former sports commentatorturned-head coach Dong Lu, CFB had scored 21 goals and conceded just two for a perfect 7-0 tournament record.

Even Dong was surprised by their success. "With 48 strong European teams from England, France and Portugal competing, our initial goal was simply to reach the quarterfinals," Dong told NewsChina in July.

CFB represents hope for Chinese football, which has struggled to score big on the international stage. The country's last World Cup showing was in 2002, where it failed to score a single goal and was eliminated quickly.

"We entered the tournament mainly to prepare these boys for this year's 2034 Cup," Dong said, referring to the annual U12 tournament he organizes in Suzhou, Jiangsu Province for the 12-year old squads from youth football clubs and schools nationwide. The name "2034" refers to the year Dong hopes China will return to the World Cup finals.

Founded in 2017, CFB scouts and develops talented players aged 12 and younger. Unlike traditional youth clubs, which are mostly pay-to-play, it provides training with professional coaches and opportunities to compete overseas, largely free of charge. Admission is highly competitive, with players selected through a rigorous, transparent process.

But CFB's approach of prioritizing skills and match experience over chasing titles has drawn criticism from China's youth soccer establishment, especially surrounding Dong's lack of coaching credentials. CFB's supporters argue that getting to participate in major competitions like Sigismondi, without simply focusing on winning them, is what benefits young players in the long run.
Young Guns
CFB's championship quickly dominated headlines and social media discussions across China. On Sina Weibo, the victory topped the trending list on June 2.
"Is this how it feels to support a top-flight football team?" a Weibo user from Liaoning Province named Hu Adi commented.
On June 3, the State-run broadcaster CCTV News shared a 21-second video showing Meng's decisive penalty kick and the team's celebration. The clip got nearly 2.3 million views by July 15.

The excitement came amid years of disappointment surrounding Chinese soccer. The ranking of the Chinese men's national team has fallen from 53rd in 1993, when FIFA introduced its rankings, to 91st in 2026. In 2025, the team dropped as low as 99th after losing 1-0 to Indonesia, then ranked around 118th in a crucial Asian qualifier for the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
Plagued by match-fixing scandals, corruption and inadequate training, both the men's national team and the Chinese Super League have struggled to win public trust.
The team of 12-year-olds has reignited hope among Chinese soccer fans.

To celebrate the achievement, real estate tycoon and businessman Li Xiaohua hosted a banquet in Beijing on June 27 for Dong and the young players. "I spent a lot on this banquet not only because I admire their championship win, but also because I have been moved by Dong's efforts over the past nine years," Li said at the event.
This is not the only corporate support CFB has received.

On July 9, smartphone maker Honor sponsored Dong's club, giving each of its young players one of its flagship phones, according to the Xinhua News Agency. Several days later, beverage company Nongfu Spring extended its sponsorship agreement with CFB from three years to five, according to Zhejiang Daily's Tide News.
"Previously, none of our sponsorships lasted more than three years," Dong told NewsChina.
Dong said over the past nine years, player
training
and
international competitions cost 58 million yuan (US$8.6m), a major chunk coming from sponsors like automaker BYD.
Dong distributed the tournament's 50,000 euro (US$57,100) winnings equally among the 14 players.

Despite its humble beginnings and criticism over Dong's lack of coaching credentials, CFB has grown from a controversial experiment into a youth training program that has earned rare recognition from mainstream Chinese soccer.
In its early years, the club had no permanent training ground. Players recruited from schools and clubs across China gathered for intensive sessions on rented pitches only days before competitions.

A breakthrough came in 2019, when Dong partnered with the Ma Yuehan Athlete Class at Tsinghua University High School in Beijing, allowing around 20 CFB players to train regularly at the school's facilities for four years.
But the school did not renew the contract. "I was devastated because it felt like all my efforts had disappeared overnight," Dong said. "What consoled me was seeing these players develop."
More than a dozen have gone on to join club programs in Spain or youth teams in China, such as with Beijing Guo'an.

Last year, eight of CFB's former players were starters on Beijing's winning U16 men's squad at the 15th National Games, including captain and defensive midfielder Li Dongchen, winger Chen Junhan and forward Zhao Songyuan, who scored the opening goal to defeat Hubei Province 3-1.

The Sigismondi Cup was not CFB's first success in Europe. In 2018, the club's U10 squad won the Wide Star Cup finals, a tournament held in Germany organized by Chinese companies Shandong Wide Star Sports and Beijing Lebo Football. Seven of the eight participating teams were European.

However, the team's 4-1 victory over Germany's Borussia Dortmund U9 squad attracted limited attention. It came during the final years of China's "golden yuan" soccer era, when billions of yuan from real estate companies and other investors fueled overseas projects and heavy spending on foreign players and coaches.

The investment brought short-term success, including Guangzhou Evergrande Taobao FC's two Asian Football Confederation Champions League titles in 2013 and 2015 under head coaches Marcello Lippi and Luiz Felipe Scolari. But the era was also marred by corruption scandals, match-fixing and misused funds.
At the time, youth development received far less attention than immediate results. Now, CFB's rise represents a path focused not on buying success, but on developing young players from the ground up.
Contested Plays
Debate over Chinese soccer only intensified after Dong achieved what many professional coaches had struggled to accomplish.

In an interview with Sina News on June 18, former Chinese soccer star Sun Jihai, a defender for English Premier League club Manchester City from 2002 to 2008, expressed concerns over CFB's frequent participation in international games, arguing that chasing results at the youth level runs counter to proper player development. "It is like growing crops. You need to wait until autumn, not summer, for the harvest," Sun said.

In 2024, Sun openly recruited young players across the country for his youth soccer club based in Dalian, Liaoning Province aimed at providing equal opportunities for talented players from all backgrounds. The young recruits attend local schools and receive free training and accommodation at the club's base.
It has nearly 90 players from ages 9 to 13, and focuses on developing fundamental skills such as ball control, dribbling and combination play.

But Sun's team has yet to win any major tournaments. On February 13 in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, the club lost 4-0 to Evergrande Football School in the qualifying final of the Universal Youth Cup International Tournament Apuane, losing access to the ensuing games organized in Italy.
On May 28, its U13 team was eliminated from the provincial qualifiers for the Chinese Youth Football League, a national competition organized by the CFA.

However, to help each club reach its full potential, the Chinese Football Association (CFA) has introduced regional tournaments alongside provincial qualifiers since 2025. As provincial runnersup, HBK qualified for this year's North Region 1 tournament, where they secured a spot in the national top 32 with six straight wins, scoring 31 goals and conceding just two.
While Sun continues to emphasize the importance of technical development, Dong holds a contrasting view.

"Sun is one of the few Chinese players to have competed in both the FIFA World Cup and the English Premier League, so his professional experience naturally shaped his training philosophy," Dong told NewsChina.

"But his achievements do not mean my experience with game-based training should be dismissed. Over the past few years, I have led CFB teams in more than 1,000 competitions, including over 400 international tournaments. There is no absolutely right or wrong approach. We have simply chosen different paths."

The debate has also attracted broader attention. On June 9, an article published on the People's Daily website argued that CFB's challenge to conventional youth training should not be dismissed as unconventional or short-sighted.

"Let's evaluate Dong's training approach rationally and let time determine whether it is scientific and sustainable," the article said. "What we can confirm now is that China should tolerate diverse training models, as long as they are legitimate and follow the rules of children's physical and psychological development."

It compared the difference in youth training approaches to the relationship between the country's professional Chinese Super League and the local amateur Jiangsu Super League in Jiangsu Province, which has achieved organic commercial success in recent years. While they serve different purposes, they are ultimately complementary.
"With both, the future of China's football development can be strengthened," the article said.
Game Sense

The 2026 World Cup final on July 20 was memorable for Spain's near-perfect tiki-taka style and Lionel Messi's emotional farewell, but also CFB's Meng Xinyi, who was a flag bearer at the opening ceremony.
For many Chinese fans, Meng represents a new generation carrying China's World Cup hopes.

"The Sigismondi Cup victory is already in the past and cannot determine anything about the future," Meng told NewsChina on July 13. "I'll cherish what comes next and continue devoting myself fully to football."
His ambition is shared by many young players across China.

Zhou Zhanxu, a 12-year-old student at Changping Middle School affiliated with Tsinghua University in Beijing, wants to become a professional soccer player. His teammate Shi Jian with Beijing Huixin Football Club said he hopes to balance academics and football because he does not want to give up either.

In June, Huixin FC sent Zhou and Shi to Japan's Nara Club, a division three professional team, for a weeklong exchange training program. Shi said it improved his ability to observe the game, make quick decisions and defend as a central defender.
"The training atmosphere was excellent. Nobody chatted or got distracted during the sessions, and I improved a lot in that environment," Zhou said.
While young players remain enthusiastic, their parents are more cautious.

"A child should grow up with a sport that can stay with him throughout his life," Shi Yiheng, a sports lecturer at Henan University of Engineering and Shi Jian's father, told NewsChina. "But becoming a professional player is another matter, because the odds of becoming a professional athlete are very low."
"I will support my son entering professional soccer only if he demonstrates not just technical ability but competitiveness as an athlete and continues pursuing his dream every day."

Zhou Zhanxu's father shares a similar view. "We respect his dream and support his dedication to the sport, but we won't push him to be a professional player," Zhou Hang said. "His health and education are our top priorities."

According to the head coach and owner of Beijing Huixin FC who spoke to NewsChina using only his surname Chai, China's exam-oriented education system forces many passionate young players to abandon soccer after primary school.

"But we don't want to simply follow the broader environment," Chai said. "Since 99 percent of the children at our club still want to continue training after primary school, we provide three training sessions and one match every week, just like at Nara Club."

In February 2024, China's General Administration of Sport issued document on encouraging the expansion of campus soccer programs and training bases. The document set a goal for China's boys' and girls' youth teams in various age groups to reach leading positions in Asia by 2030.

A year later, the number of registered amateur soccer players aged 21 and under reached 109,220, an increase of 16,241 from the previous year, according to the Chinese Football Association. However, the figure is less than oneseventh of Japan's registered players, the People's Daily reported.
Following Meng's performance in Italy, his hometown of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province said it would support his overseas training, his father Meng Qinghua told NewsChina.

"The local government and school promised to preserve Meng's enrollment status if we decide to send him abroad," his father said. "That gives us an important safety net if overseas training does not work out.'

"Our family discussed this carefully. We know overseas training will be challenging and that standing out will not be easy. But we do not want to let such a valuable opportunity pass without trying."

title: AI Companions: Our Friends Electric
subtitle:
More than productivity tools, robot makers are aiming to create
ultra-bionic humanoid companions capable of providing emotional
comfort - and raising some uncomfortable questions among
regulators
byline: By Wang Shihan, Yu Yuan and Yi Ziyi
paragraphs: In the 2013 sci-fi film Her, Scarlett Johansson voiced "Samantha," an AI operating system that formed a deep emotional bond with the film's protagonist.
More than a decade later, UBTECH is among the latest companies taking a step toward embodying that vision.
At its 2026 global launch event on June 30 in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, the AI and robotics company unveiled its UWORLD U1 series, a lineup of full-size, ultra-bionic humanoid robots.
The robots, standing between 1.60 and 1.85 meters tall, made their debut with a runway show before waltzing with human dance partners.
Designed for companionship, each comes with large language models geared for emotional development, encrypted memory storage and customizable appearances.

UBTECH is far from the only Chinese startup entering this field. Unlike humanoid robots designed for manual labor, these companies focus on creating human-like facial features, skin texture, voices and body temperature, while training robots for emotional interaction.

But as these robots increasingly resemble human companions, the boundaries of "companionship" are becoming less clear. Their attractiveness, ability to emote and capacity to simulate bonds put them somewhere beyond the conventional role of a machine. In some cases, companionship may naturally evolve into romance or intimacy, possibilities that are raising new issues for lawmakers about how the industry should be regulated.
Awaiting Orders
For years, humanoid robots were primarily developed as productivity investments that generate high returns. But companies like UBTECH are betting consumers will pay a premium for a friend.

Its new U1 series ranges from the 119,800-yuan (US$17,696) half-body Lite to the flagship Ultra, which has autonomous locomotion and enhanced computing power for up to 999,000 yuan (US$147,568). They also come with male or female appearances.

Speaking at the launch event, Zhou Jian, UBTECH's founder and CEO, said the industry had previously focused on whether robots could perform household chores. Today, however, he believes people increasingly seek companionship, happiness and emotional fulfillment.

His view reflects broader demographic trends. According to the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics, China's adult single population surpassed 300 million in 2026. That figure is close to the population of the entire US (342.7 million) and exceeds the combined populations of the UK, France and Germany. Nearly one in four Chinese adults is now single.

China is also aging rapidly. According to the National Health Commission, the country's population aged 60 and above reached about 320 million by the end of 2025, accounting for roughly 23 percent of the total population. The commission projects that figure will exceed 400 million by 2035.

Zhou argues that industrial humanoid robots risk becoming little more than hardware products with limited ecosystem potential. But consumer humanoid robots could generate not only hardware sales but also long-term subscription revenue, making them more profitable over time.

On launch day, UBTECH received 13,361 orders, with deliveries slated for September 16. Assuming every order was for the entry-level U1 Lite, that equates to more than 1.5 billion yuan (US$191m), or about 77 percent of the company's total 2025 revenue. UBTECH aims to produce 10,000 U1 units this year and expand annual production capacity to 50,000 units by 2027.

Toward the end of the launch event, UBTECH demonstrated several of its human-faced robots on stage. Videos shared online showed noticeable mechanical stiffness while walking, as well as clear differences between the robots' real-world appearance and the polished promotional renders released earlier, prompting some netizens to accuse the company of misleading consumers.

Jiao Jichao, UBTECH's vice president, said in an interview at the launch event that the greatest technical challenges in building highly lifelike humanoid robots lie in the head. These include facial muscle movements, coordinated neck motion and binocular vision for eye tracking, all of which require extremely precise control and synchronization.
Uncanny Valley
When it comes to ultra-bionic humanoid robots, prioritizing physical attractiveness is an unwritten rule.

At an office in Shenzhen's Nanshan District, our reporter met Suyan, a female robot developed by Shenzhen Yizhizai Intelligent Technology. Designed for emotional companionship, Suyan is scheduled to be delivered to its first overseas customers in October.

Two Suyan models are displayed in the company's lobby. One sits on a chair wearing a blouse and high heels, while the other stands against the wall in a sporty, casual outfit. Tall and slender, with soft skin and carefully applied makeup, Suyan can be mistaken for a real person from a distance.

Wu Heng, Yizhizai's founder, told NewsChina that the team's priority is not hardware specifications or movement performance, but how well the robot matches users' vision of an ideal companion. To achieve that, the company analyzed preferred facial features, voices and personalities from users of Chinese and overseas social media platforms.

Suyan targets male and female users between the ages of 35 and 55. According to the company's research, this group prefers a sophisticated, empathetic and emotionally mature female companion. The team aimed to give Suyan an air of affluence and success, while having the calm temperament of a therapist.
