On July 13, the State Council, China's cabinet, approved the 15th Five- Year Plan for Expanding Consumption, which sets a 2030 retail sales target of 60 trillion yuan (US$8.85t), nearly 20 percent higher than the 2025 level.

The plan, the first of its kind, sets out 28 key tasks across six areas, with a strong focus on boosting household spending power and expanding services consumption. It calls for more stable employment, higher minimum wages and greater household property income, while pledging to strengthen social security and increase public spending on education, healthcare and eldercare to ease household burdens. The plan seeks to raise the share of household spending on services through expanded offerings in eldercare, childcare, culture and tourism, health and sports.
How these plans are implemented will be crucial in determining whether China's
K-shaped
divergence
will persist.

title: Film: Tickets to: Paradise
subtitle:
A new animated film gives
Taoism's Eight Immortals a very
human origin story, and sends
curious tourists looking for their
mythical home
paragraphs: In Penglai, the legendary paradise of Chinese mythology, the gods have KPIs to meet.
They clock in for work from 9 to 6 every day, receive performance evaluations and are assigned temples according to the amount of incense their worshippers offer.
When a mortal makes a wish, the gods are expected to fulfill it, no matter how absurd the request. In one scene, a worshipper asks for a rooster to lay eggs.
This is the irreverent world of All Wishes Come True!, a new animated feature that reimagines one of China's best-known folk legends, the Eight Immortals.

Produced by Pearl Studio, the creatives behind Kung Fu Panda 3, Abominable and the Oscar-nominated Over the Moon, the film tells the origin story of the eight legendary figures by presenting them not as powerful immortals, but as a ragtag crew of characters who manage to outwit powerful gods and ultimately earn their divine status.
The
approach
went
viral

on social media. Positive buzz from advance screenings prompted producers to move up the film's release a week to July 18. It went on to gross 400 million yuan (US$58.9m) in its first five days and had reached 1.1 billion yuan (US$163m) by August 2, making it the highest-grossing animated film of the summer season.

But despite its commercial success, the film has caught criticism. Some have taken issue with its depiction of deities in the Taoist pantheon, raising debate over how far filmmakers can reinvent a traditional legend before audiences push back.
Legends in the Making
The Eight Immortals is one of China's most iconic folk legends, appearing in oral traditions, operas, paintings and literature over the centuries.
The best-known story, "The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea," is detailed in the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) novel Dongyouji (Journey to the East) by Wu Yuantai.

Each is a legend in his own right. Li Tieguai is a beggar with an iron crutch who heals the sick. Bare-bellied Zhongli Quan has a magic fan that can revive the dead. Eccentric Zhang Guolao rides his white mule backward. The group's leader, Lü Dongbin, wields a magic sword that repels evil.

After attending a grand gathering of immortals on Mount Penglai, the crew decides to return to the mortal world by crossing the East China Sea. To make the trip, each demonstrates their unique magical abilities: Li Tieguai turns his crutch into a boat, Zhongli Quan floats on his fan and Zhang Guolao rides his donkey on the waves.

The tale spawned the common Chinese idiom, "When the Eight Immortals cross the sea, each displays their own magical powers," which is used to describe people drawing on their individual talents and strengths to accomplish a shared goal.

Part of the Eight Immortals' appeal comes from their humble origins. Unlike other heavenly deities, they are mortals from different backgrounds who attained immortality through cultivating virtue and overcoming hardship.
It is this largely unexplored period of their lives that director and screenwriter Mu Zhengyang wanted to bring to the screen.

"Everyone has heard the story of ‘the Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea,' but very few people know what they actually went through before attaining immortality," Mu wrote in an article published in the People's Daily. "So we want to fill in that missing chapter."

The film begins with Taoist swordsman Lü Dongbin enlisting Zhongli Quan, a cursed wanderer living as a thief, to break into the divine treasury on Penglai and recover a magical lamp. Along the way, they recruit six more companions who together plan to pull an Ocean's Eleven-style heist while posing as immortals.
Their change from schemers to celestials is central to Mu's adaptation.

"In my view, the Eight Immortals are a rare group in Chinese mythology that embodies ‘mortals attaining immortality.' They were not born as deities, nor did they possess innate magical powers," Mu wrote. "They were ordinary people who emerged from the mundane world, each with their own background, trade and flaws."

The film takes that idea further by giving Penglai a touch of the mundane. Instead of an infinite paradise, Penglai is a sprawling bureaucracy. Heavenly officials deal with complaints, chase quotas and struggle with the trivial frustrations of office life. Interestingly, Taoist traditions themselves often portray the heavens with departments, officials and courts that mirror the earthly realm.
The joke has landed well with younger audiences, who shared their stories on social media comparing the film's Penglai to their own workplaces.

"That scene where Cao Guojiu (an administrator in Penglai and one of the Eight Immortals) makes a routine office call and has to fake a polite voice while not smiling was so relatable to an office drone like me," Yvonne commented on RedNote.
Film critic Chen Tong called it one of the film's most creative elements. "The concept is both funny and an imaginative fusion of mythology and contemporary life," he told NewsChina.
Just Like Heaven

The film also impressed viewers with its striking visuals. The animation team drew inspiration from classical murals, traditional color palettes and landscape paintings to create an aesthetic that feels both authentically Chinese and distinctly modern.
According to Mu, the film's signature iridescent look, from the immortals' outfits to Penglai itself, comes from descriptions in ancient Taoist texts.

"They often describe immortals as ‘radiant and shimmering with flowing light,' and we translated that imagery into a visual language suited to contemporary audiences," Mu wrote. "The immortals' robes shimmer as the light changes, capturing the ethereal elegance of classical depictions while showcasing modern craftsmanship."

Mu added that, in designing Penglai, the creative team referenced the colored glaze and gemstone textures of the Malachite Inlaid Jewel Penglai Fairyland Landscape, a Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) artifact housed in the Palace Museum in Beijing.

"The iridescence is a refined take on traditional folk culture. It preserves the bold colors of New Year paintings and the rustic textures of folk artifacts while reinterpreting them through modern aesthetics and technology," Mu said.
Combined with the blue-green palette of traditional shanshui landscape painting, Penglai takes on the warm, translucent luster of jade, the director wrote.
Down to Earth
The film's Penglai may be legend, but the name belongs to a real place.

Penglai, now a district in the city of Yantai, East China's Shandong Province, has long been associated with the mythical island where the Eight Immortals are said to have gathered before crossing the sea.

The film appears to be giving that connection a fresh boost. According to travel platform Tongcheng Travel, searches and bookings for scenic attractions in Penglai rose by more than 70 percent year-on-year in July. Visitor numbers and spending on dining, accommodation and cultural products have also increased, according to the platform.
Local authorities have been quick to capitalize on the interest. The Yantai Bureau
of
Culture
and
Tourism announced that moviegoers can receive discounts or free admission at nearly 20 scenic spots across the city by presenting their ticket for the film.
Among the attractions is Penglai Pavilion, a site built in 1061 and associated with the Eight Immortals' legendary journey.

The story is also poised to cross even larger seas, with All Wishes Come True! slated for screenings in more than 10 countries and regions in August, from the US, UK and Australia to Papua New Guinea and Luxembourg.
Keeping it Real
The film received widespread praise from both critics and audiences, earning an 8.2 out of 10 on Douban, China's leading film review platform.

"A fantasy film in appearance, a heist film in structure and a martial arts film in spirit. This time, it moves beyond the familiar rallying cry of ‘I am the master of my own fate' and instead tells a grounded, heartfelt story about human relationships. It's a remarkably successful genre film," wrote Douban user Tianmaxing.

"What excites me most is that Chinese animation finally has a story worthy of such stunning visuals. The suspense is sustained throughout, and the twists in the middle and at the end are both surprising and satisfying. Although the story is largely original, it captures the essence of the legend: the Eight Immortals are ordinary people from the mortal world, each with a distinct personality," wrote another user Lixiaodiu.
Nevertheless, some viewers criticized the film for misrepresenting revered figures from Chinese mythology such as Yang Jian, a god known for his truthseeing third eye.

"The film portrays Yang Jian as a ruthless villain who wants to use a magical lamp to sacrifice all mortals in an attempt to resurrect his deceased mother. That goes too far. In Chinese mythology, Yang Jian is a hero and a protector of humanity," Yang Xin, a 28-year-old from Hunan Province and an avid Hanfu enthusiast with a strong interest in Chinese mythology, told NewsChina.
Yang also took issue with the film's rendering of the Three Gods of Fortune, Prosperity and Longevity, which are among the most widely worshipped Taoist deities.

"Many people still display their statues or portraits at home. But in the film, they are depicted as greedy, selfish and unlikeable. I think that portrayal shows little respect for our traditional culture," Yang said.
Some of the criticisms have more to do with storytelling. Critic Chen pointed to inconsistencies in the characters and their motivations.

"The film presents the Eight Immortals as flawed, self-interested people, but it doesn't provide enough key turning points to convincingly explain how they become such a close-knit group. The transformation isn't fully developed," Chen said.

"Characters such as Li Tieguai begin as selfish swindlers motivated purely by money and treasure. Yet in the second half of the film, they suddenly become willing to sacrifice their lives to save humanity. That shift in motivation feels abrupt and unearned."
The debate reflects an age-old problem filmmakers face when revisiting ancient myths.

British director Christopher Nolan's retelling of the ancient Greek epic The Odyssey has drawn criticism for its departures from Homer's text. Released the same weekend as All Wishes Come True!, it similarly stirred controversy for its changes to characters, events and the role of the gods.
Though different in their approaches, both directors faced the same challenge of choosing what to preserve and how to bring new life to the tale for modern audiences.

For Mu Zhengyang, the choice was returning to its human core. After all, the Immortals were once ordinary people. "And that is precisely the most fascinating part of their story," Mu wrote. "They each had their own agendas, undermined one another and argued constantly. Yet it was precisely these imperfect people who, at critical moments, chose to stand by one another and turn the impossible into reality."

title: Pickleball Diplomacy: Serving up Friendship
paragraphs: ifty-five years after Ping-Pong Diplomacy helped break the ice between China and the US in April 1971, pickleball is now writing the next chapter of bilateral people-to-people exchange between the two countries. In February, Jeffrey Sullivan, systemwide athletics director for Montgomery County Public Schools in Maryland, US, led a 45-member youth pickleball delegation to China during the Spring Festival, traveling from Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province,
to
Beijing,

experiencing authentic Chinese culture along the way. In April 2025, Sullivan led a pickleball delegation of 44 teachers and students Ffrom 13 US schools to China for the first time, under Chinese President Xi Jinping's "50,000 in Five Years" initiative that aims to bring 50,000 young Americans to China for exchange and study programs over five years.

Pickleball is a fast-paced sport, but easy to learn, according to the USA Pickleball website. It is played indoors or outside on a badminton-sized court, in singles or doubles, using a paddle and plastic ball with holes in.

After visiting Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing, the delegation sent a letter to Xi, expressing their gratitude for the initiative. In his reply in early July 2025, Xi said he was pleased to see that pickleball has become a new bond for youth exchanges between China and the US. In return, young Chinese students from Shenzhen and Shanghai visited Montgomery and several other places in the US, including Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Washington, DC, in 2025 and 2026 to continue the friendship of young people from the two countries on and off pickleball courts.

Sullivan has frequently described his Chinese trips as "life-changing" for the students and himself. Recently, Sullivan told China News Service (CNS) how pickleball can boost people-to-people exchange between the two countries and continue the bilateral connection formed by Ping-Pong Diplomacy more than five decades ago.
Sullivan
stressed
that

cultural exchanges have made their visits "more than a trip," noting that more than a year since their first trip, students from the US and China are still communicating through WeChat. All those friendships and experiences are "genuine," and that's the "cool part of it," he said.
China News Service: What was your impression from the two visits to China?
Jeffrey Sullivan: My understanding and my experiences in China have been incredible. I've used the word "magical" before. The hospitality we received on both of our trips was amazing.

On our first trip, going to Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing, pickleball diplomacy was really born. The connections that were made, the friendships that last to this day and will continue, and the ability to embrace Chinese culture really made a strong impact on us in that first trip.

The second trip, returning to Shenzhen and having smaller city experiences like Shangyou (Jiangxi Province) and Hebi (Henan Province), and returning to Beijing, was just next level because we visited during the Spring Festival. Being able to celebrate that holiday in China was simply out of this world.

What really said home for us was how many Chinese people, at every stop, during a time when they were supposed to be resting, relaxing and spending time with their own families, were making us feel at home and feel like family.
My experience in China has been incredible, and I'm very excited to return there soon.
CNS: Was there a particular moment in China that touched you?
JS: I don't know if there was one particular moment. I think it was watching the countless friendships between our student ambassadors and their friends in China every step of the way.
That started immediately when we got off the bus at the first stop on both trips. Watching that happen, I was overwhelmed with joy.

Being on the Great Wall of China with my daughter is a moment I'll remember for the rest of my life. She grabbed me by the shoulders at one point and said, "Dad, close your eyes." I closed my eyes, and she said, "We're on the Great Wall of China. I don't want you to ever forget this moment."

I had tears in my eyes. There are a lot of memories on the trips, but I think the hospitality and the welcome we got in every location have been incredible. It's something that has set the stage for pickleball diplomacy to continue to be successful.
CNS: What makes an experience like this so powerful that you've described these trips many times as "life-changing?"
JS: I think it's traveling around the world to a new country that, for most of our ambassadors, including me - last April was my first time in China - and embracing another culture and learning.

And for me, it's not just about the trip. What's made our initiative so successful is the lead-up to each of these trips, the preparation. It's no different from preparing for a big game in sports, all the practices and the preparation. When it comes time for the game, you play well. In addition to pickleball events, the most important part was the cultural learning sessions that we had and the preparation for the trip. Those activities created a third thing - relationships, and building a family among our delegation. That created strong bonds between our [student] ambassadors and between the adults and me as well. And when we arrived in China, we were able to focus solely on building relationships, embracing culture and being part of a life-changing experience.
CNS: Why do you think firsthand experiences like these are so important?

JS: Because the experiences are genuine, so you're able to see people. Despite the differences in cultures, politics and all the things between countries, the roots are the people. Having that people-to-people connection and building those relationships and understanding culture and taking an intentional interest in learning someone else's culture is a powerful thing. It's a life skill that doesn't just apply to the US and China. It applies to here at home in your school, in your community, with friends and with co-workers.

Those are life skills about taking an intentional interest in someone else's culture who may be different. How do you build a relationship? And how do you identify similarities and build bridges? I believe that through pickleball diplomacy, we're embracing those life skills and the mindset that has allowed our student ambassadors to change and grow.

I've heard the phrase "life-changing" being used countless times with our student ambassadors and with their parents, and with me. This experience has changed my life and my outlook on a lot of things. I want to continue to make those life changing experiences for our student ambassadors and for countless people.
CNS: What is the biggest challenge your students face when they are trying to understand China?
JS: I think initially it's more of not knowing, not understanding the history, of the culture of China and learning that piece of it. I think it's more of unknown versus a negative perception.
What we look for in our [student] ambassadors is the willingness to learn about culture and about China. So that's been part of our preparation for our trips.
CNS: Of all the possible ways to connect young people, what makes sports, pickleball in particular, so effective?

JS: Sports bring people together. They bring countries together. You can see that on the grandest stage, the Olympics, where nations come together every four years to compete and join together. That's the international level. You can also see here at the high school level how sports play an important role in school culture in bringing the school communities and the schools together to compete.
I believe in the power of sports to bring people together and showcase the ability to learn, to celebrate wins and to handle defeat with dignity.

So you learn all the lessons in sports in teamwork. That plays into a sport like pickleball. One of the things about sports is that people are afraid to fail. Or sports sometimes can be hard to pick up and master. Pickleball is a sport that's easy to pick up. Because of that quick entry point, the ability to quickly pick up a paddle and experience success, most people can get through that anxiety period rather quickly.

We've had [student] ambassadors on both trips who had never played pickleball before. But they picked up a paddle and said "I like this. This is cool." And the sport itself plays out perfectly for something like what we're doing, because a doubles team plays a doubles team - Chinese and Americans play side by side. They play in this team and they compete on the court. And what we see is instantaneously the teamwork, the sportsmanship, the special handshakes, the tapping of the paddles. And they communicate on the court, like who's going to be on what side. All of that happened quickly. So pickleball emerged to be a great sport because of that. The competition occurred, and the friendships were still there.

For us, in Montgomery County Public Schools, we were the first school district in the US to have pickleball as our city sport. That's what initially brought attention to us and opened the door for pickleball diplomacy to happen.
CNS: What role do youth exchanges play in the future relationship between the two countries?
JS: I would 100 percent encourage more youth exchange programs. I think it provides an opportunity to learn, to grow, to build a shared understanding for the future. Our youth are the future.
Sports are one pathway. But there are also opportunities through the arts and music as well. There are a lot of ways to connect. I think the more we can connect, the better.
For us, in one small way, all the relationships we built are building bridges and building bonds. The world is a happier place when we are doing it. We're happy to be part of it.
CNS: Ping-Pong Diplomacy has lasted for 55 years. Looking 20 years into the future, what do you hope today's students on both sides will remember about their journeys?
JS: I hope all the friendships are continuing to grow and blossom.

I hope that they carry the memories that they have with them and also tell the stories. I think it's important to tell the story of what pickleball diplomacy was about. So my hope is, as I said at the airport after our first trip, "The trip may be over, but our legacy will live on."
Whatever that legacy is, I think it's been a positive one to this point of being an activity and an experience that builds bridges and bonds and friendships that are genuine.
Our students use the term "aura" all the time - the aura around you, the vibes of what you do. So we talk about the aura of pickleball diplomacy.

It's not just about pickleball, or diplomacy or about sport. It's the aura around. It's the connection and the feeling. So you live pickleball diplomacy. That's what we say and we believe our [student] ambassadors have brought that to life.
My role is to create the spaces for that to happen. I help lead and get out of the way to let our students do their thing. That's been the cool part of it.
It's gonna be cool to watch it and continue to build.
This article was originally published by W.E. TALK, a China News Service production. Reprinted with permission from CNS

title: Chinese Museums: Collector's Items
paragraphs: Museums are gateways to the past. They are places where objects, stories and ideas allow us to step beyond the boundaries of our own time. It's why I have always loved museums, and thankfully, China has an extraordinary variety of them. Indeed, many of the world's largest and most visited museums are in China. From the 7 million annual visitors who experience the massive National Museum of China in Beijing which covers almost 200,000 square meters, to the 6 million visitors who enjoy the 85,000 square meters of the Nanjing Museum, in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, China has plenty of megamuseums to explore.

In fact, according to the Themed Entertainment Association (TEA), 14 of the top 20 museums in the world are in China, with the three most visited museums in the world all in the country. According to TEA, the Louvre Museum in Paris, France, long regarded as the world's most visited museum, has now been overtaken by the Palace Museum (Forbidden City) in Beijing, which sees 17 million annual visitors, while the honor of second-most visited museum in the world has been claimed by Chengdu Wuhou Shrine Museum, with Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum in Xian, Shaanxi Province, coming in third.
Gallery to History

However, China is also home to many smaller, less internationally famous museums, which are often rather unique. In many ways these smaller museums offer an even more intriguing insight into Chinese life and Chinese culture than their larger cousins. One of my favorites is the Former Qing Dynasty Post Office, which is in Zhujiajiao Ancient Water Town near Shanghai. Although the museum covers only 70 square meters, it offers a fascinating glimpse into how daily life in China slowly modernized across the eras of the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), the Republic of China period (1912-1949) and the early stages of the People's Republic of China (1949-present).

Another fascinating museum is Gulangyu Piano Museum, located on Gulangyu Island, Xiamen in Southeast China's Fujian Province. This intriguing museum presents, displays and promotes the island's unique musical tradition, which fuses European and Chinese elements. The museum includes two separate buildings, which are filled with an assortment of rare and magnificent pianos including everything from miniature models to elongated grands. Many of the items in the collection feature intricate and colorful designs. The Piano Museum is directly connected to Shu Zhuang Garden, an eccentric paradise of curiosities, with a single ticket required for visitors to enjoy both attractions.

China also has several major museums that are dedicated to specific historical figures or events. These include the Museum of Dr Sun Yat-sen in Zhongshan and the Opium War Museum in Dongguan, both in South China's Guangdong Province, and the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution in Beijing. These museums highlight the incredible importance of certain events and individuals in shaping the course of Chinese history. Spending time understanding these museums and their contents is one of the most accessible ways for international visitors to better appreciate how the events of the past have shaped modern Chinese people and modern Chinese culture.

For those interested in Chinese military history there is no shortage of museums to whet their appetite. Within the category of military history, my personal favorite is Zhongshan Warship Museum in Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province. This museum has been entirely constructed around the SS Zhongshan, a massive Chinese gunboat built in 1910, which was sunk by the Japanese in October 1938 during the Battle of Wuhan. The wreck was salvaged from the bottom of the Yangtze River on January 28, 1997, before being relocated to its present site. As a time-capsule, visibly representing an important period in Chinese history, the Zhongshan now stands at the heart of this fascinating museum. Today, the monumental ship is surrounded by the stories of those who experienced the terrors, virtues and upheavals of that pivotal era.
Jurassic Past

However, not all museums in China are dedicated to the story of human history. Some of the most fascinating museums in China are part of the country's collection of natural history museums. Established museums include the Chengdu Natural History Museum, Sichuan Province, which includes one of the largest substantially complete dinosaur fossils in Asia, the Chongqing Natural History Museum, which has an excellent collection of Jurassic-era fossils, and the Shanghai Natural History Museum, one of China's leading museum attractions. I should also add to this list the Shenzhen Natural History Museum in Guangdong, which only opened in July 2026. Although I have not yet had the chance to visit this new museum, it promises excellence, with a massive building area of over 100,000 square meters. Nevertheless, of all the museums in China dedicated to nature, the National Natural History Museum in Beijing remains my personal favorite, in large part thanks to the ginormous and terrifying animatronic dinosaurs, which inhabit the atrium's jungle.

If you are looking for something a little more offbeat, unusual or quirky, there are plenty of curious and unusual museums and exhibitions in China. One that I enjoyed recently is the Nanyue King Museum in Guangzhou, which includes an extensive exhibition of ceramic pillows. Needless to say, the idea of sleeping on a cold solid block of ceramic directly challenges every notion of comfort and sleep that I have learned in my life thus far. However, my favorite "niche" museum in China is the Yak Museum of Lhasa, capital of Xizang Autonomous Region, which charts the extensive, historic and symbiotic relationship between the yak and the people who cohabit the plateau.

Fortunately, there are still plenty of other unique museums that I am yet to explore, but keen to experience. Morbid fascination means that I am especially looking forward to visiting Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Museum in Urumqi, which comes highly recommended in part due to its display of well-preserved, and interestingly dressed, corpses known as the Tarim Basin Mummies. I also have a (possibly unhealthy) curiosity about the China Abacus Museum in Nantong, Jiangsu Province, which claims to be the foremost museum in the world dedicated entirely to the abacus. However, the next museum I intend to visit is the China Watermelon Museum in Beijing, which celebrates China's long and intriguing relationship with watermelon cultivation, and probably deserves the prize for the oddest and most niche museum in all of China.
Practicalities

Tickets to Chinese museums can be bought through travel platforms like Trip, museum mini-apps on WeChat or at the museum itself. Some larger museums will require identification such as a passport and reservation in advance, such as the National Museum in Beijing or the Palace Museum. Special exhibitions may cost extra. onestly, I never really gave this much thought until recently. When I did, I just shrugged and figured it was some quirky little habit unique to my family. But then I started noticing it everywhere and found plenty of people online pointing it out, too.

If you've spent real time around Chinese folks, you'll inevitably spot this hilarious, almost automatic ritual that kicks in the second it's time to sleep. No matter the weather or what they're wearing, they will always make sure that their belly button is under wraps. It's a whole phenomenon.

It happens even on sweltering summer nights, when the AC is broken, and you're practically melting into the mattress, arms and legs sprawl every which way to catch any whisper of cool air. Yet there's always that one tiny anchor: a thin sliver of blanket, the folded hem of a T-shirt, or in moments of sheer desperation even a scrap of tissue paper standing guard over that one tiny spot on the stomach. It's honestly kind of comical. A person can be completely starfished, a sweaty mess, but peek closely and that navel is safely tucked away.

I remember when I was a teenager, when crop tops were the absolute musthave. I wanted to look cool, but my internal alarm bells would ring the moment a draft hit my navel and I'd inevitably end up with diarrhea afterward. So, I did what any resourceful (or slightly paranoid) teenager would do, I slapped a giant Band-Aid right over my belly button. I looked ridiculous, but guess what? I never once got a stomach ache after a night out. I was a weird evil genius!
So, what's the real deal here? Why the collective panic over a tiny hole in the middle of our stomachs?

Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has a poetic answer. According to TCM, that little divot is actually a major energy hub called the shenque acupoint. Unlike the rest of your torso that's shielded by muscle and fat, the navel is pretty much the thinnest membrane in the neighborhood and a direct highway to your digestive organs.

There's even an old saying that "illness enters through the belly button," meaning cold and dampness can waltz right in while you're blissfully unconscious. And when you're asleep, your defenses are napping too. Your pores are wide open and your yang energy is taking a break which, according to TCM, turns you into an easy target.

Before you write this off as ancient mumbo jumbo, modern science actually gives a respectful nod to grandma's old sayings. The abdomen is packed with temperature-sensitive digestive organs. A sudden chill on that bare spot can trigger spasms, mess with your gut rhythm, and leave you bloated the next morning. So keeping that area warm overnight isn't just superstition, it's basically a low-tech heating pad strategy our ancestors figured out through everyday observation.
But honestly, growing up, I didn't do it for the science. It's a habit written into our emotional DNA.
